utterances.text: That is also, I presume, a very terrible and strong experience. So tell me, please: Why there's no mention at all about this experience in your statement given in September 2000. You didn't mention it with one word, that while you were leaving your house and headed for your neighbour's house, all this was happening. Did you also consider this not to be important?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, the investigator didn't ask me such a detailed question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that, then, correct, that the investigator never asked you anything about the events that took place on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he did ask me about some incidents, but he didn't go in so much detail as you are doing now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you gave a very elaborate description of everything that was happening in your flat, in your neighbour's houses, but this particular event that there were shellings -- there was intense shelling while you were going to your neighbour's house?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in so many details, but since I made a solemn oath, I confirm now that that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you think it wasn't important to mention?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not asked in so many details by the investigator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Grbic, I have no further questions for you. I would like, at the end of this examination, to tell you, on behalf of my client, that he is very sorry about everything that you and your family had to endure in terms of psychological and material losses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with this, I have concluded my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just a few matters, Your Honour. Re-examined by Mr. Weiner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during your testimony, they asked you if you heard about members of the Croatian army being in the Old Town, and you said: Yes, on Srdj, St. Blaise, and Lapad." Actually -- and you also said Gradac park and Bogisic park. Are any of those places you mentioned in the Old Town? Srdj, those parks, or those places?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever seen Croatian troops in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever heard of Croatian troops in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those places that you described that you heard where the Croatian troops were, let's take the two parks. Gradac park. How far is Gradac park from the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gradac Park is approximately 700 metres or 800 metres from the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Bogisic park? I don't think I have the right pronunciation. But something like Bogisic park?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogisic park. Bogisic park is even further away, between 800 and 900 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to show this witness a copy of map P12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And if they could place this on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that map, sir, that area depicted on that map?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the layout of the Old Town of Dubrovnik and some of the suburbs around the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please show us where Gradac Park is.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't see on this map, because it is somewhere here. Because this is the Lovrijenac fortress, from which, as I said, the edge of the park is some 40 metres away, and this park covers this whole area, and this distance across the sea, about 40 metres. So if you add another -- the width of the fort times three, then we can reach the distance which I just said. That is all together more than 700 metres. So if you add these two distances, you will get the distance from the town to the Gradac Park.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please, with a marking pen, place a 1 -- could you please place a 1, the number 1, in the area where the Gradac park is.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you show us first where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before we leave that, could the record disclose that a mark has been placed actually in the margin around the map, not on the map itself, because the park the witness indicates is not actually depicted on the map itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you now place -- first show us where the other park is, Bogisic park.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogisic park. Which number shall I use? Number 2?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A further mark made by the witness, again in the margin, because it is his evidence that both parks are beyond the area depicted on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to offer that map, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it not already an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's already Exhibit 12, but since 12 has already been marked, or 12 is being used as kind of a plat, we'd like to offer that as a new exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, allow me, please. We object to this item being entered into the files because there's actually nothing that you can see. You have just two marks on the margin that don't signify anything. And another thing: If we are to proceed in this manner, then we should see a bigger map and have the witness indicate these locations on the map. Otherwise, I don't see any point in doing this in this way. Maybe this is not the right moment, but I would also like to pose one more question after Mr. Weiner has finished, and it concerns exactly what he is asking the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I'm inclined to agree with Mr. Petrovic. It seems to me that you have from the witness his evidence that the parks are at the distances he's given from the Old Town, that they are not depicted on the map because they are beyond the margin of the map. And is that not enough for your purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's enough for the record. However, Your Honour, I think the record should be clear, because this witness was asked several questions about Croatian troops, and the record should be absolutely clear that the Croatian troops and the mortars that he mentioned and those items or those things that he saw on those public-domain videos, which are public-domain news broadcasts which he videotaped or had a friend videotape and give him a copy were not in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're in the process of identifying that with him, and you have dealt with the area of the two parks, and he has made clear that neither of those are within the Old Town. I think that evidence and the transcript of it is clear. I don't think that the matter is going to be assisted by receiving that plan as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Petrovic, you had something else you wished to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. I'm not sure if Mr. Weiner has completed his examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Oh, I thought you wanted to raise something before he went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I merely wish to ask the witness two additional questions later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Weiner. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Counsel asked you about a - thank you - about an armoured vehicle. Did you ever see that armoured vehicle depicted on the video in the Old Town, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He also asked you about this three-barreled machine-gun or anti-aircraft gun. Did you ever see that in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you're a noted figure within the Old Town of Dubrovnik. Did you get a chance to speak with a lot of people during the fall of 1991, fellow Old Town residents?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did people pass information and gossip about what was happening?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People talked about ferocious attacks in the surroundings of Dubrovnik, in Dubrovnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a vehicle, an anti- -- a vehicle with an anti-aircraft gun was driving through the Old Town, would you have heard about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, that's stretching admissibility. Don't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: They asked you about certain military commanders. Did you see -- ever see any Croatian military commanders walking through the Old Town in October, November, or December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified yesterday that you were out with your sister when an explosion occurred, and this is in October of 1991. And you returned to your house after that explosion?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you looked out the window, you saw the Rupe Museum had been damaged?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a hole in the roof of the museum, caused by a shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sometime after that, did you hear some sort of whizzing sound?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the other side of the house, the one facing east, on Siroka Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do after you heard the whizzing sound?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I threw myself on the floor of my own room, backwards. I fell backwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hear any noise after that?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Immediately after the whirring sound of the shell, I heard an explosion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you look out the window to see what damage was caused by that explosion?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw pieces of roof tiles outside on the street, but I couldn't see more damage, because that was behind me, on the roof. I could only see that once I came out into the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whose house was damaged, the roof tiles and the roof?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Mr. Pecar's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know who was living in that house?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His relatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you knew them?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I have your patience for two or three minutes, by your leave, of course?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You wish to ask more questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two other questions, in connection with the map that has just been shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two minutes, not more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'll start my stop watch now, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take my word for it, Your Honour. Can the witness please be shown Exhibit P --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the -- P12. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Petrovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Grbic, do you know about maps?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, quite well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see the proportions indicated, the scale indicated in the lower left corner of the map?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point out the Bokar tower on the map for the Chamber? Can you point out where the Lovrijenac fort is on the map? By using this scale from 0 to 200 metres, from the western corner of the Bokar tower and the eastern corner of the Lovrijenac fort, what is the distance?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About a hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The Bokar tower, is it in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's part of the town wall, as you can tell by looking at the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Lovrijenac tower, is it part of the cultural and historical heritage of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not part of the wall, but it is part of the town's cultural heritage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that should amount to about 140 metres between the Bokar tower and the Lovrijenac fort?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I look at it now, it seems even more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just another question. Can you please have a look at the upper left corner, Anice Boskovic Street, this small green area indicated on the map.

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the Bogisic park?

utterances.speaker: IVO GRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's just one section of the Bogisic park.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we please have the record reflect the following: The document P12 was shown. In the upper left corner of the document there's a green area. The witness indicated that this green area next to Anice Boskovic Street is a section, in fact, of the Bogisic park.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there anything further, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Grbic, I'm pleased to be able to tell you that that's the end of your evidence. Thank you very much for coming and for the assistance that you've given to us, and you are now free to go and do whatever you wish. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Before the next witness is called, I would like to introduce a member of our staff, a new member of our staff, from the Sydney Australia bar, barrister David Re is with us. The next witness will be called, Mr. Mustac, and Ms. Gina Butler will be handling that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Butler. If the witness could be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would please take the affirmation now, Mr. Mustac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd be seated. Ms. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before Ms. Butler starts, Your Honour, could I just inform Your Honours that the Prosecution has in Court with us today, seated on the side, a legal intern working with us from Australia, Ms. Yasmine Ahmed, A-h-m-e-d. Ms. Butler will take the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Examined by Ms. Butler:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Would you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Ivan Mustac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: The 17th of December, 1935.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I'm a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you lived in 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: In 1991, I lived in the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this in the area of the Old Town? Did you live in the area of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: In the Old Town, that's where I worked. On the 14th of October, as of the 14th of October, I also resided within the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll talk about that. What is your -- what was your occupation in 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I was the head of the state archive at the Sponza Palace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your title?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I was the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And how long did you hold this position as the head of the historical archives of the Sponza Palace?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: From 1991 to 2000.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you the director before the shelling in 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were your qualifications for that position?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: According to the law governing the rules and archives, I had taken a state exam and I had an MA degree as a librarian and expert in archives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the director, could you also tell the Court what your responsibilities were.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: My responsibilities were governed by the law on archives. I would draw up a programme, a yearly programme, and I would see it through, make sure that it was carried out. I would inform the ministry of culture, the central authority on the progress of this programme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Directly to the ministry of culture, to the minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir: Were you required to work at the palace on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you ever held any political appointments?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What appointment did you hold? What position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Croatian parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were you -- were you elected into the parliament?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I was elected on the first democratic elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I need to consult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. Let's go back. When were you elected?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: In May, early May, 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were elected in 1990, how long did you hold this position in the parliament?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: A full term of office, until 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, before --

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I turn to my next section of questions, I'd like to ask permission from the Chamber to present the witness with the previous Prosecution Exhibit P13. I understand that the reintroduction of this exhibit will require a new exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to discuss the Sponza Palace, where you were the director of the historical archives. Using the map, can you tell us where the palace is located, giving us the street address and maybe circling it on the map? Sir, you might want to use the map itself, to your left -- I'm sorry, to your right. Sir, can you put a number 1 inside of that circle, annotating the Sponza Palace.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: For the record, please note that the witness has circled and put a number 1 by the location of the Sponza Palace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, how old is this building, the Sponza Palace?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: The Sponza Palace was built in 1520.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the architectural features of the building?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: It's a mixture between Renaissance and Gothic. It was built by native architects and sculptors or carvers from Dubrovnik, Pasoje Milicevic and the Andrici brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please describe for the Trial Chamber the function of the Sponza Palace in 1991.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: In 1991, the Sponza Palace housed the state archives. It was referred to as the historical archives at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the significance of the archives?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: The archives represent a memory of a nation, of a town, of a country, its roots. All civilised countries hold their archives in high esteem and hold it dearly. This is also a UNESCO World Heritage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe the specific contents of the archives, some of the contents of the archives?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: The peculiar nature of the Dubrovnik archives was their continuity, meaning that all the documents had been preserved, even in their entirety. The first document dates back to 1022. The archives of the Dubrovnik Republic, obviously, are also there, everything that was relevant for the work of an independent country like that, until the country ceased to exist, in 1815.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you: How important is the Sponza Palace to the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: The Sponza Palace is the second building of the Dubrovnik Republic, in terms of its administration, in terms of its architectural style, in terms of its official rank, it ranks among the most eminent buildings in the Old Town. I would say the rector's palace was the most important one, and the Sponza Palace comes a close second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there or has there ever been a military function associated with the palace?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: No, never, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to spend some time with 1991. Specifically, what precautions did you take when the war began in 1991 to protect the archives?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: We received assistance from the ministry of culture to protect the windows with sandbags. In the cellar of the palace itself, we put away the most valuable documents from the archives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you first start taking these precautions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Immediately, in October, after some parts of the town had been attacked, such parts as Mokosica, Brgat, and Ploce, these sections of the town. However, these are not within the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you actually move the archives? Did you ever move the archives from the Sponza Palace?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let me ask you: Were you in the Old Town, sir, on the 23rd of October?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I was at work, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe what happened that day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: The first attack took place on that day, the first attack on the Old Town. I heard sounds of explosions, and I didn't expect that the Old Town would be attacked, the historical town centre. Therefore, I was quite surprised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you surprised that the Old Town would not be attacked?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: The Old Town, in its entirety, is a UNESCO World Heritage site. It became a UNESCO World Heritage site back in 1989. There were plenty of refugees all over the town. At that time, people who had fled Konavle, more than 6.000; at least that's what people said. And everyone believed that the Old Town itself would be spared, the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that you were at work when the shelling began. Were you inside or outside your office, or the building?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I was in my office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what time was this when the shelling began?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I think it was between 11.00 and 12.00 o'clock. I can't be certain, however, that this is the exact time. It may have been a little earlier or a little later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did it last? How long did the shelling last?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: It didn't last long. If I have to specify this in terms of time, I cannot be quite sure that I'm able to say that. But it seems to me that I heard a series of explosions, a sequence of explosions, and then it was all over, perhaps within two minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know there was shelling?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: We heard a tremendous explosion, and in the atrium of the palace we found a large number of shrapnels. After a while, I went out of Sponza and I had been told that the shell landed to a nearby street, towards west, and that was Boskovic Street, which was rather near. I went there to see for myself, and I saw that it was true, and I saw the damage inflicted by the shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Approximately how many shells did you hear?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: It's difficult to say now how many there were. Quite some time has elapsed since then. But I think that that was a series of linked explosions, and I had a feeling that there were more than one of them. Whether two or three, I cannot say now for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Was there any damage to the archives?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: At that time, only parts of the shells, meaning shrapnels, damaged the roof, and we found pieces of the shell in the courtyard of the palace. But the palace itself did not sustain any considerable damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally walk around the building and inspect the damage?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That is why I said that the only damage was caused to the roof and the roof tiles. But other than that, no other major damage was caused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Did anything significant happen the following day, say the 24th of October?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: That was on the 23rd of October, and the following day was the 24th of October. And there was also shelling on the 24th, but I myself didn't hear the explosions close to the very core, centre of the town. Yes, we did hear explosions, and I know that one shell landed in the Old Town port, but I honestly cannot tell you how many of them were fired, and I even didn't know then, because I never asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know about what time that shelling began?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I can't remember precisely now, but it seems to me that it occurred approximately at the same time, at or thereabout, at noon or thereabout, one hour, plus or minus. Please allow for this tolerance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, let me ask you: Do you know a Mr. Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes, I know Mr. Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was he, sir? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: He was a JNA colonel and a commander of the Trebinje garrison. Trebinje is a town close to Dubrovnik. And he had undertaken the task of organising the defence of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, what is his first name?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: His first name is Nojko, Nojko Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have any communications with Mr. -- I'm sorry, with Colonel Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I knew him well, and we met on occasions and talked to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have talks with him in November? Did you speak to him in November?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the nature of those communications?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: The 1st of November, I was preparing myself to go and attend the session of the Croatian parliament, and I wanted to take the opportunity to travel on the so-called Libertas Convoy, from Dubrovnik, which was under the blockade at the time, to Rijeka, and then onwards to Zagreb. And Colonel Marinovic then told me that he had a very important message for General Tus, for me to convey to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that message?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: He virtually told me the following: "Please tell Mr. -- General Tus that Dubrovnik has no ammunition, no weapons. Tell him that we have one recoilless gun. And with that, Dubrovnik is unable to defend itself."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you able to deliver this message to the General?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the General's response?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I met with the General in Zagreb, in Tkalciceva Street. Before that, his headquarters had been shelled. It was -- it used to be situated on Dubravkin Put in Zagreb. The General received me. He didn't have any insignia upon him. I knew him from photographs. He put his hand on my shoulder and told me the following: "Sir, whatever Croatia has at its disposal at the moment, if we were to transfer that to the Dubrovnik theatre of battle, that would be too little, because that is incomparable to the power and force that the Yugoslav army surrounding Dubrovnik has." Then I asked him: "What are our prospects, our chances? What do you think?" He looked at me and said: "I truly don't know."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you attend a parliament meeting in November?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes. The session was held on the 8th of November, and I attended this session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you get there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I sailed on a ship from Dubrovnik to Rijeka, and then in a car from Rijeka via Slovenia, to Zagreb, and this car belonged to the deputies of the Croatian parliament who resided in Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I understand that the parliament met in Zagreb. What was discussed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: The only and the most important item on the agenda was the declaration of independence of a sovereign state of Croatia and the severance of all relations with the then-Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And where did you go after the meeting in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I sought a possibility to transport humanitarian aid that had already been collected in Rijeka through the offices of the Red Cross and the Caritas charitable organisation, and for that purpose I asked the ministry of the maritime to place a ship at my disposal. They said that they could do that but that they couldn't issue me a permit for that. Then I sought assistance everywhere. I asked the bishop, Koksa, that -- but he also replied that he was unable to provide this kind of permit for me. Since at the time an international acumen congress of religious organisations was taking place in Zagreb, a friend of mine, Zdravko Mrsic, drew that to my attention. The venue of the congress was the Intercontinental Hotel. I went there, and I was -- I was told that there I could find the president of the All European Jewish Community, Mr. Jean Cahn. I asked him directly if we could sail under the Jewish flag and to ask them to request this on our behalf from the Jewish community and thereby allow us to transport the humanitarian aid from Rijeka to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to get this aid back to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes, we were. The Jewish community charged Mr. Jakov Bienenfeld, member of the Jewish community, with the task of providing this permit without me being involved in that. He got the permit through General Raseta, and it was signed by Admiral Brovet. The permit provided that only a five-member crew could be on board the ship, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir: Who was General Raseta?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: General Raseta was at the time the commander of the 5th Military District, if I remember correctly. I cannot say for sure whether he was the commander or the deputy commander. And he was a liaison officer through whom we managed to obtain this permit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. When did you return to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: We set sail on or about the 15th of November, and we reached Dubrovnik on the night between the 17th and 18th of November. Usually, journalists reported that it took place on the 18th, because that was the day when they arrived and saw this ship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you remain in Dubrovnik in November?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: After we took the humanitarian aid to the shore - and the name of the ship was "ILIRIJA" - I took the next ship, which was "LIBURNIJA" and I returned to Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you return back to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I returned to Dubrovnik on the 26th or 27th. It was night again. But I arrived there after terrible difficulties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... difficulties, sir?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: On board the ship, I had fallen ill. According to the doctor's diagnosis, it was salmonella, and the ambulance was waiting for me on the dock because the captain sent the word to the shore, and I was taken to the hospital, where I stayed until the 4th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you -- you told us that you reached -- I'm sorry. You told us that you contracted salmonella, you were in the hospital, you came out on the 4th of December. Did you hear anything significant that may have happened in the Old Town in November?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: While I was in hospital, my friends came to see me and told me that, on the 13th of November, a major attack was launched on Dubrovnik and that many buildings, many landmarks were damaged during the attack. Of course, I was most interested to hear what happened with the Sponza. They told me that its roof had been hit in several places, that the wall carvings were damaged, that the Franciscan, the Dominican monasteries were also damaged, including the cathedral, and other palaces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, after you were released from the hospital, did you personally inspect any of the damage to the Sponza Palace?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes, although my health condition was not exactly good. I went there and I saw not all the details, but on the following day I scrutinised it more carefully and realised that the Sponza Palace -- that the roof of the Sponza Palace had been hit on the east side, on the south side, and on the west side. But those surfaces had already been covered with PVC sheets, due to which the palace was protected from the rain. But there were no roof tiles replaced as yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And during the October and November shelling incidents, did you file any official reports?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: My duty was, because as the head I bear both moral and material responsibility for whatever is housed inside the archive building, not the building itself only. So I duly filed a report to the minister. But the same report had already been submitted by other institutions that were responsible for this kind of reporting, and by that I mean to the Institute for Protection of Monuments. And there was another institution of the Association of Friends of Dubrovnik, who were engaged in the reconstruction of Dubrovnik. However, the most official report went from the Institute for Protection of Historical Monuments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, were you aware of any communications between the Croatian authorities and the Yugoslavian authorities regarding the shelling?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: A commission was established in the town of Dubrovnik, an official commission, which communicated with representatives of the Yugoslav army. Secondly, there were European observers in the town, who also communicated with the JNA. And thirdly, cultural institutions, such as the office of Mr. Federico Mayo [phoen] was operating in the town. Mr. Mayo was the UNESCO director. For several months, Mr. Bruno Carnez and Mr. Kaiser were in the town, and I also had communications with them. These two gentlemen sent their reports to UNESCO about the damage that Dubrovnik had incurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you participate in any of the official communications?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I only participated in the work of the commission, which just recorded the damage sustained by the palace. It was my duty to open the door for them, and they were not allowed to do an inspection in my absence. Other than that, I had no other communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Were you aware of any letters of protest sent to the Yugoslavian authorities?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: The mayor of Dubrovnik, and other cultural institutions, including the bishop of the town, sent daily letters to all renowned personalities, whether it be politicians, artists, and other known figures all over the world. And I knew everything about this campaign, because I was at such a place where I could be at the source of all these events. Anyway, all these letters have been published in a book entitled "Dubrovnik in the War, Between 1992 and 1993."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let us turn to the 6th of December. You told us you were in the hospital when you returned from Rijeka, until the 4th of December. Where were you on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, I was in my flat - sorry - in my friend's flat, in Zamanjina Street number 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened that day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: That is the day which left a terrible impression on me, and I may say that ever since then I have become a different person emotionally. As far as I can remember, the shelling started before 6.00 a.m. Shells were falling on the town, and all of that woke me up. I instinctively, because I was living on the worst position floor. It's a house with three floors and I was on the third floor. I went down to the ground floor. All the old Dubrovnik houses have a kind of arch on the ground floor. Usually the floors are made of wood. And in this vault, in fact, I found a family with two children and two elderly -- and an elderly couple, and I was a seventh individual in this space which we may call a kind of shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in that shelter?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I must say that it seemed to me an eternity while the shelling was going on. The time virtually stopped for me. Because I thought myself to be outside any time or space. My only thought was when I'm going to die. But I did feel that the shelling became intermittent, and it happened at around 11.00 o'clock, when I noticed that the shelling was landing apart from one another. I ran out, and I wanted to reach the Sponza Palace because I knew that I had a safe shelter there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, from where you were staying, how far away was the Sponza Palace?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: About 40 metres. It depends from which direction you look at the palace. The west side was closest to me, and it was about 40 metres away. If we talk about the eastern or southern side, then it's further away. So I can say that it was 40 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can we use the map. And I'd like to ask you to circle the street that your residence was on. Can you use the letter "A", showing your residence.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And sir, did you eventually reach the Sponza Palace?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you notice on your way to the palace?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: In this spooky space, I met a young man on the corner of Dropceva Street, who told me that -- in fact, he asked me: "Where are you going? You're going to get killed." I didn't say anything to him. I just turned away. But I recognised the young man as Pavo Urban. He was the son of a colleague of mine. She was the chief librarian and I was the head of the archive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Urban again?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: No, I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come to learn anything about Mr. Urban?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: This horror and hell of shelling stopped at about 4.00 p.m., if I'm not wrong. But I can't tell you exactly. I didn't look at my watch. Most probably I never looked at my watch. But I do remember that it was still daylight. I went out. There were people already in the streets. And the first -- my encounter with those people was horror and fear on their faces, and some of them told me that Pavo Urban had been killed. That happened on the south side of the palace, and there's an arch there. Looking from the east, from the direction of Ploce, there is in fact a niche and a jeweller's store and he probably sought shelter there, and that is the place he was found dead. That was the first information I heard about Pavo Urban.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, thank you. Did you observe any damage to the Sponza Palace when you came out?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: It's difficult to say what I observed. It's a horrendous situation when your reason cannot function, especially in people who are not skillful in wars and waging wars. I only saw the smoke on the main street, which is called Stradun, and I saw fire at the end of the street, where there's a square. The whole town was shrouded in smoke. One could feel a very strange odour. It's difficult to explain. And the wind was terribly strong. It was cold. So that would be generally, if we are going to put this into Judo-Christian terms, an apocalypse. And something had fallen from the skies, and you never knew whether it was going to hit on your head or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, were the archives damaged?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I only saw that the next day. I had a more careful look. That evening, all my attention was on the fire that was raging through the town. The next day I realised that there was major damage too. The worst damage was to the roof. The side of the roof facing west, about 30 square metres. The side facing south, about 12; and the side facing east, about 10. The side facing south has a supporting beam, and this beam was blown to smithereens. This is built in wood. The Sponza Palace has an axis which stretches in a north/south direction, and the side facing south is entirely made of wood, whereas the side facing north is made of reinforced concrete, due to various problems related to landslides. But I don't think we should go any further into this now. The reinforced concrete plate supporting the wall to the west was severely damaged, and the supporting wooden beam broke. The cement coating displayed cracks. The archives themselves, however, the files, were not damaged. There was more damage in the courtyard. The plastic sheeting, the architectural ornaments, especially on the side of the courtyard facing north, the monogram of Christ, or a eulogy to Dubrovnik measures, which is a text that is carved into the wall of the courtyard. The capitals too were damaged, the Acanthus leaves and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice any other damage to other buildings or palaces in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, there were palaces across the town that were ablaze. It was there for all to see. It was only later that you could realise that more damage had been done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you to mark these buildings on the map in alphabetical order, the buildings that you saw damaged and the palaces that you saw. Can you also tell us the name of the street?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Here we have the street known as Od Sigurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you circle that street and use the letter "B."

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take us to the next street, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Can you walk us through this map that you've made for us. You started off with Od Sigurate Street. How many buildings or palaces were damaged, did you see?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Two palaces. One is the Festival Palace, and the other one is the adjacent one that had caught fire after the Festival Palace had been hit. So it just caught fire. I believe that the fire did not break out because it received a direct hit, but it caught fire from the other building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you take us to the next street.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: The next street is between the palaces. This is a residential building and cannot be placed in the same category as the palaces. This would not be the highest category. It would not be classified as A, but rather, as B, in terms of cultural heritage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of the street or the area?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: The name of the street is Izmedju Polaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And the next street?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: The next street is Miha Pracata. There's another palace there. I think it's at number 6. The next street is Od Puca, number 11 and number 16, I believe. The next street is at the corner of Siroka, number 6. And the next one is St. Joseph's Street. Also Od Puca, and the last one is Zlatariceva Street, but this is another residential building, so I don't think it would be given top priority, such as a proper architectural palace, a monument of culture, would be. It's not equally valuable. So seven palaces, all in all, and two residential buildings, as I would call them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, as you walked -- as you did a walk-about throughout the town, did you find any fragments or shells or any shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: At the Sponza Palace, my palace, I found shells, which I picked up and stored away in the cellar. I retired in 2000. I believe that those shells are still there as some sort of testimony to something which I never want to see happening again. There was also a lot of shrapnel that we didn't pick up. In addition to those palaces, I saw many other damaged buildings, such as, for example, the monastery of the Little Brethren, the Franciscan monastery, St. Blaise cathedral, St. Blaise and the cathedral, the pavement of the main street, which also has a great historical significance. There were craters drilled by shells, and they stayed there for a long time before the street was re-paved. The general idea -- and of course, I'm speaking after seeing the reports, being no expert myself. It is generally believed that over 50 per cent of the buildings inside the Old Town were damaged, over 50 per cent, that is. I believe that is the figure. The figure was 58 per cent, I believe, but certainly it was over 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any idea of the monetary costs for the repairs to the Sponza Palace?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Each and every report of the special commission contained all the costs specified. I remember that the figure was over $100.000 at the time, or 100.000 German marks. I can't be sure now, however. I do believe that the sum was expressed in dollars, and it was an amount over 100.000. 107.000 or 108.000, I believe. That's only the damage to the Sponza Palace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, I just have a few more questions for you. Did you see any military presence in the Old Town during October, November, or December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: The Old Town was a civilised place with a lot of history, and always in the town there were police officers upholding law and order, and obviously there was a police presence in the town. I saw two funny individuals carrying rifles of sorts, funny-looking rifles, at the Pile gate, on the western approach to town. And at the other gate, the Ploce gate, to the east. I used to visit often, even later, because a curfew had been imposed. Someone told me to stop right where I was. I looked at that funny-looking man and I smiled. I said to myself: My God, what is this? Are these supposed to be our defenders, with weapons like that? At any rate, that's what I saw. Furthermore, I saw uniformed people moving about town, but those were locals. But they didn't reside there, nor was there any kind of barracks in the town itself. They just came and left. So in answer to your question, that would be about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Did you see any outgoing fire from the Old Town on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: No, no. No, I didn't. Not only did I not see anything like that, but by virtue of my position in my official capacity, I would have known had anything like that happened. But I was simply not aware of anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I notice the time is 12.30. Would you like for us to take a break? I just have a few more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: All right. I was waiting. I thought you were able to finish. But we'll have the break and then finish after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There will be a break of 20 minutes, Mr. Mustac, and if you could continue then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, I want to remain within my time, but I just want to clarify a few points with the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I notice that you made reference to buildings being classified as A or B. Can you tell us what these classifications refer to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: It is generally known that monuments of culture are classified in categories starting with 0, which is World Heritage; A is National Heritage; B is Environmental Heritage; and C is a lower category. You might say that peculiar features of a certain region are classified as monument C.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is a UNESCO classification or a local classification?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about this being official UNESCO classification, but that's all I know about it. Regarding the distinctions between various monuments of culture. The Old Town itself, the historical Old Town centre, referred in Latin as Intra Muros has been classed as UNESCO World Heritage since 1979. Therefore, each individual part of this heritage is under special protection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, speaking of UNESCO, were there any UNESCO flags flying in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were UNESCO flags inside the Old Town, as well as the official UNESCO emblem, a well-known one, which was all over these buildings that I spoke about, those classified as A monuments. The Sponza Palace, certain monasteries, the cathedral, St. Blaise. Not each and every building bore this sign.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when they were put up, the flags were first put up?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically when, but I can say that when I arrived in town in mid-October, the flags were already there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Just a few more questions. I'd like to clarify the map that we've annotated with the different buildings that you saw damaged. Can we go back to the map? What I'd like to do is take another walk through the map. I'd like for you to put on the record the street names. I'd like you also to think about what these buildings were used for. Were they religious, were they residential, were they cultural, or were they works of art and science. If you can help me with that, I would appreciate it. Okay. Let's start with building -- the first building that we marked.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: The first two buildings are on Od Sigurate Street. One was the headquarters of the Dubrovnik Summer Festival, and the other was a residential building, locally referred to as a palace. It was not a public building. It was privately used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a residence?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: All the other buildings -- yes. All the remaining buildings were residential buildings, just that in the ground floor there's usually a shop or a bar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Okay. For the record, we've marked Od Sigurate Street, with the - I'm sorry - with the letter A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought the witness was referring to the buildings marked B and C. Am I wrong? Each of the buildings are marked alphabetically from B to I. The building A was where Mr. Mustac was sleeping --

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- on the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to building A. Building A is the building that you were sleeping in?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the name of the street?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Zamanjina Street. That is by and large a residential street, or rather, residential building, with family flats, and that's where I lived. It did not have any public use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to letter B.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: That's Od Sigurate Street, which is where the headquarters of the Dubrovnik Summer Festival were located. This building had an official use, a public use, a cultural institution. The building next to it was another residential building which did not have any public use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's go to letter C.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: This was a residential building, or palace, between -- or rather, in Izmedja Polaca Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us whether this building was dedicated to religion, charity, and education, the arts and science, or historic monument or work of art and science?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: You mean the building marked as C?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: It was a residential building. As far as I know, at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's go to building D.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: This was also a palace with its own features, architectural features, of course, and that's why it was classified as a palace, but it was used for residential purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And the name of that street?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Miha Pracata Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's go to letter E.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes. This was also a residential building in Od Puca Street, or rather, this is the corner of Od Puca Street and Siroka Street. It's a residential building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's go to the letter F.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: This is also a residential building. The street is Od Puca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's go to the letter G.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: This is also Od Puca Street. I think the number is 11. This is a residential building. It didn't have any public use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue on to the letter H.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: This is also a residential building on Zlatariceva Street. It's not a public building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following on with the letter I.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: This is what we refer to as St. Joseph's Street. This is also a residential building, with shops on the ground floor. These shops were well known, the shops on this street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've given us some additional buildings that were damaged, particularly the monastery. Was that used as a religious function?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes. The Franciscan monastery and the Dominican monastery are famous monasteries in Dubrovnik. They have very famous libraries, where many manuscripts are kept, as well as valuable old books.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the Franciscan monastery? Was it active, an active building?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The monastery is adjacent to the church, which was a place of worship and used as such. Mass was celebrated there. That's the church of the Little Brethren, as it was known. And the monastery also houses a library, a world-famous library, that was unfortunately damaged. It was early this month that the reconstruction was completed and the books were returned to their place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, the St. Blaise cathedral, was that an active church?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: St. Blaise is not the cathedral. That's a different church. It's a church the patron saint of which is St. Blaise. The cathedral is another church, as I said, and both churches were hit, but mass was celebrated throughout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, to make the record clear, would you mind changing the number 1 on the Sponza Palace to a letter S, for clarification.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And sir, I also note that we have not marked the place where you saw Pavo Urban at his last time [sic]. Can you mark that with the letter X.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, when you finished walking around the Old Town on the 6th of December, what time did you return to your home?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I had no home to go to, to begin with, because on the bed where I slept there was a shell lying on the bed itself. It had fallen through the roof. And I was put up by the other residents in the house, so I stayed with them. I returned. If I can have the Honourable Chamber's understanding on this. I was not exactly looking at my watch. This was the furthest thing from my mind. I was quite shocked overall, and I felt as someone who was about to get killed himself. I returned in the evening. It may have been about 7.00 o'clock in the evening, when all other people went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just two questions, sir. Going back to the UNESCO flags: Were they also flying in November and in December? I think you said you may have saw them in October. But when -- were they also flying in November and December?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes, throughout, throughout the entire time, the flags were there, in October, in November, December, and January. They were never removed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. My last question for you: Looking back at this shelling in October, November, and December, how did it really make you feel? How did you feel?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: This is very difficult for me. I felt desperation, hopelessness. I felt as if I would never see my nearest and dearest again. I was not aware of their fate at the time. I cried. But not only I cried, everyone cried, everyone I came across. If you ask me what my thoughts were at the time, I prayed, and prayed. Being a believer, all I could do was pray. But I refused to hate. I refused to hate even those who, God knows why, had fired the shell that fell on my bed while I was away. It was a dreadful moment in life, but I have since become a different person, and I view the world in a different manner now. It was some sort of catharsis for me, a cleansing experience. I wish this had never happened, and I wish this never happens again to anyone. I wish it were possible for everyone to live in peace, in love. We are all human. The race doesn't matter. I don't think I am alone in believing this. I am certain that there are many people who share this belief of mine. So this, for me, is one of the results of the war. In this case, it is a positive, desirable result.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for your testimony. Sir, I would ask you to sign the map, put your name on the map, give your signature and today's date. And then, Your Honours, I'd like to offer this map into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received when the witness has completed his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Prosecution Exhibit P39.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my testimony -- I mean, my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Butler. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May I please have the Court's indulgence? Can I have the lectern please. It would make my cross-examination a lot easier. As unfortunately we only seems to have this one lectern in the courtroom to go around. Cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Mustac. My name is Vladimir Petrovic. I represent General Strugar before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mustac, please tell me: Have you ever set eyes on a document known as preliminary report on the damage to buildings in the Old Town of Dubrovnik, dated the 6th of January, 1992? This document provides a detailed account of all the damage caused to the Old Town in October, November, and December 1991.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I believe I saw this document, if that is the document signed by architect Matko Vetma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me: When was the last time you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I saw it before I arrived in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see it during your stay in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I have a copy of the document on me. I've had occasion to look at that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the document that was signed by Ms. Paula Kolic and Ivica Zila.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you reviewed this document, did you see exactly -- what does it say? When was an on-site investigation conducted, precisely, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I didn't pay attention to that particular detail, but I will agree with whatever you say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says that an on-site investigation was carried out on the 10th of December, 1999 [As interpreted], giving the exact time of day. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that on examination-in-chief you said today that there had been an earlier on-site investigation. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I don't know that I said that. What I said is the following: There were commissions that arrived, whether officially or not, on a daily basis, and every day we would have a look. This institute for the protection of monuments of culture and nature and the state archives were under the same roof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This report dated the 10th of December, 1991, signed by Ms. Kolic and Mr. Zila, as the title of this extensive document would seem to indicate, damage caused in the time period of October, November, and December 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This report, does it also indicate which damage was caused in October, which was caused in November, and which in December? Does it distinguish between the three different months?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes, there is a certain amount of distinction, but not a very detailed list. As far as I remember, the focus was on the destruction of the 6th of December, and there are also photographs of destruction that occurred on the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these photos that were made after the 6th of December, later on, in other words?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Perhaps a day or two later, on the 7th, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all right. It doesn't make any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the usher's assistance, please? I would like to show the witness a photograph. This photograph is from a 65 ter Rule exhibit, Exhibit 35. This is the east wing of the Sponza Palace. Can you please place this in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you have a look and tell me if this is the photograph we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether what we're looking at here, at the top of the photograph, is this the damage you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes. The white bits where the roof tiles are missing, this is merely a photocopy, so the white areas would be the holes that were covered over with nylon sheeting of some sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the photograph from the same document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us: What can we see on this photo?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: This is also the left side, and there is some kind of hole in the middle and on the end. So one may conclude that this could have been some kind of damage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any other damage on this part of the building, or is that all, what we have seen on these two photos?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: If I compare this photograph with the first one, then I couldn't say that these holes are identical. So I couldn't say that this is an identical photograph, whether it was made before the 6th, or on the 13th of November, now I cannot say exactly, but I must say that they were not identical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you noticed on the previous photograph, and on this photograph as well, a difference that I'm sure you must have noticed it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. Sir, I'd just like to ask Defence if you can give us a reference or page number or ERN number that you're referring to these photographs so that we can look at them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. As I said, it's 65 ter document, marked 35, ERN, for the first photograph, was 10169839. And this one, this photograph, is 01069838.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you notice that this damage here on this photograph, this hole, is not covered with plastic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereas the previous two holes were covered with the plastic sheet as a sort of protection?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I fully agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why one part of the roof was protected while the other wasn't? Was there any reason for that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: The reason was - and I do notice that - this is a report which refers on the 6th of December, but also for the period between the 8th and the 13th of November, and also 23rd and 24th October. Therefore, there could be a confusion. Because in the legend, it does not say that this particular damage was caused on a particular date. This is my interpretation of that. So I stand by my statement that on the 6th of December, the damage which I described was caused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that the first two holes were probably inflicted earlier, in November or even back in October, and that this last damage was probably caused in December?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I categorically deny that. Why I say no? Because I was an eyewitness. Latin proverb: I saw it myself and heard many things. I said that the south wing, or rather, its supporting beam, was smashed on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please let's not go back to this. Let us try and be as concise as possible. If you think I'm wrong, just say that I'm wrong so that we can proceed. So how do you explain that some of the damage was not protected and the other was protected?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: I construe this by assumption that this photograph was not -- it was not dated the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell me, or do you remember --

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... document for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, thank you. I just wanted to hear whether the witness knows anything about this. Otherwise, it's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present during the on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
utterances.text: No. I was present -- I have to clarify this. I was present when the commission visited the scene, but I did not -- I was not present there while they described the situation. There was no need for that. I had other commitments of my own. It took a long time. They took measures and performed other acts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did it take?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MUSTAC
